title: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
desc: Requires validated scoring, controlled environments, cost and uncertainty measures, with automated judges separately evaluated.

kps.k: Agent benchmark scores measure performance under a protocol, not professional competence or deployment readiness by themselves.
kps.d: The cluster challenges the inference from leaderboard success to practical usefulness. A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents and AI Agents That Matter argue that tool-using systems need tests of sequential decisions in changing environments, rather than static answers alone. The Law of Evaluation illustrates the context problem with bar-test performance as a proxy for legal reasoning. More realistic coding and workplace tasks broaden coverage, but do not establish general professional competence. The evidence varies: AI Agents That Matter reports experiments and reproduction studies; the survey synthesises prior research; the governance papers advance review-based and methodological arguments.

qs.q: Such evaluation must go beyond measuring LLM textual outputs to assess an agent’s capacity for sequential decision-making and operation within dynamic environments.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: LLM benchmarks typically consist of input strings and rely on strings    as outputs, whereas agents often involve dynamic interactions with environments such as the web    or a command line, which are not easily reducible to static inputs and outputs.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Comparability requires validated scoring, controlled environments and clear attribution of performance gains.
kps.d: AI Agents That Matter reports inconsistent HumanEval modifications, false-success scoring in LATS and STeP, and WebArena rate limits and autologin defects that changed outcomes independently of capability. Its reproduction of an LDB baseline yielded 89.6% across five runs against a published 75.0%. The survey recommends varying foundation models, agent infrastructure and modules independently. TheAgentCompany supplies a practical quality-control example: screenshot evidence, lead-author code review, final manual checks and checkpoint review by someone outside task curation. Its supplied excerpt reports methods, not performance results. Together, these accounts support validating evaluators and documenting protocols before comparing leaderboard entries.

qs.q: For example, both LATS [65] and STeP [47] marked    some incorrectly completed tasks as correct.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Future work should develop controlled evaluation protocols that vary each factor independently, enabling systematic comparison and isolating the contribution of individual components, whether LLM capabilities, harness design, or specific modules such as memory or planning, to overall agent performance.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Realistic interaction, unseen-task testing and benchmark maintenance solve different validity problems.
kps.d: The survey favours dynamic environments for exposing cascading errors and maintained benchmarks for addressing saturation and obsolescence. AI Agents That Matter separately identifies missing hold-outs and the possibility of directly programming test-specific shortcuts into agents. It recommends hold-outs matched to the claimed level of generality, potentially kept secret. Its prediction that STeP would perform much worse on unseen websites is conditional, not an experimental finding. The survey recommends WebArena for dynamic interaction, while AI Agents That Matter criticises its missing unseen-task tests and drift modelling; these positions concern different properties rather than an unqualified disagreement over benchmark quality.

qs.q: Dynamic environments, conversely, allow agents to interact with a live or simulated world (e.g., Docker containers for SWE, browser sandboxes for web agents), where their actions alter the state the agent observes, enabling diagnosis of failure modes in long-horizon tasks.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: This is a much more serious problem than LLM training data contamination, as knowledge of test samples can be directly programmed into the agent as opposed to merely being exposed to them during training.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Useful comparisons must measure accuracy alongside operating cost and statistical uncertainty.
kps.d: AI Agents That Matter argues that repeated model calls can buy higher scores without demonstrating better agent design. It reports cheaper simple baselines outperforming many complex agents on HumanEval and a modified DSPy system reducing HotPotQA cost without reducing accuracy. The survey extends cost reporting to tokens, API expenditure, latency and evaluation itself. NIST's draft guidance treats test coverage and repeated trials as budget–statistical-power trade-offs, with repeated trials helping quantify sampling uncertainty. AI Agents That Matter estimates that a full SWE-Agent evaluation could exceed $8,000 per run and suggests, without establishing causation, that expense contributes to missing error bars.

qs.q: Therefore, agent evaluations must be cost-controlled; otherwise it will     encourage researchers to develop extremely costly agents just to claim they topped the leaderboard.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Future evaluation frameworks should integrate cost efficiency as a core metric, tracking factors such as token usage, API expenses, inference time, and overall resource consumption.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Automated judges promise scalable diagnosis, but their validity remains a separate question.
kps.d: The survey recommends execution-level metrics because final success rates conceal reasoning, tool-selection and recovery failures, while warning that isolated-step scoring can miss dependencies. Reference-based scoring offers reproducibility but can exclude valid alternative paths; LLM judges offer flexibility with reliability trade-offs. Agent-as-a-Judge proposes richer intermediate feedback and cost-effective evaluation of code-generating systems, but its supplied excerpt provides no quantitative validation. NIST warns that judge design and quality materially shape results when an LLM alone grades outputs. Xpertbench's supplied material contains only references, so it adds no evidence that these judging approaches work.

qs.q: Many current benchmarks rely on coarse-grained, end-to-end success metrics that, while useful for gauging overall performance, fall short in diagnosing specific agent failures.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: It not only retains the cost-effectiveness of LLM-as-a-Judge but is also equipped with agentic features, allowing it to provide rich intermediate feedback throughout the entire process, as it acts as an agentic system.
qs.a: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Benchmark limitations can understate assisted usefulness as well as overstate autonomous capability.
kps.d: AI Agents That Matter argues that tests concentrated on unsupervised completion omit useful human feedback and intervention. It cites Shi et al., rather than its own experiment, for a GPT-4 programming result rising from 0% to over 86% with simple feedback. The authors qualify human-in-the-loop evaluation as costly and dependent on user skill. NIST also identifies allowed attempts and feedback as evaluator-controlled settings. The practical implication is to specify the intended supervision level and test that workflow: autonomous performance and human-assisted performance answer different adoption questions.

qs.q: Thus, the lack of human-in-the-loop evaluation of agents might lead us to underestimate their usefulness (whereas the lack of held-out test sets leads to overoptimism).
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Execution Environment Scaffolding or Task For many agentic benchmarks, the evaluator determines the number of submission attempts an agent is allowed for a test item, as well as the type of feedback given to the agent for incorrect submissions.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Better benchmarks support governance, but the governance reviews reject benchmark-only assurance.
kps.d: The survey distinguishes repeat-run robustness from privacy, access-control and other policy compliance, recommending penalties for success achieved through prohibited actions. Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? argues that quantitative benchmarks cannot currently supply safety and capability assurances alone or primarily, and recommends complementary red-teaming and bug-bounty programmes. The Law of Evaluation welcomes broader safety and impact metrics but maintains that context mismatch, leakage and drift remain. This marks a difference in emphasis between improving benchmarks and recognising their residual limits, not a call to abandon them. The interdisciplinary review also rejects citation counts as sufficient evidence of trustworthiness and argues that transparent, continually validated standards can shape development because developers optimise against them.

qs.q: Beyond robustness, enterprise agents must adhere to strict policies, such as data privacy and access control, which are rarely tested in standard benchmarks.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The legal-tech-vendor evidence does not establish a substantive position on the proposition that agent benchmark scores are protocol-bound and require validated scoring, controlled environments, cost and uncertainty measures, and separate evaluation of automated judges. The sole supplied source, Xpertbench, merely lists bibliographic references to agent benchmarks and evaluation methods, including LLM-as-a-judge work; it provides no original findings, methodological commitments, critique, predictions or recommendations from which acceptance, extension or rejection of the proposition could be inferred. Because this is one item in a curated corpus and contains no substantive argument, neither common reasoning across legal-tech vendors nor material internal variation within that professional voice can be assessed.

The selected academia and research sources accept the proposition that protocol scores alone do not establish real-world competence or deployment readiness, and collectively develop it into a more concrete evaluation agenda. Their common reasoning is that agents operate through sequential interactions in changing environments, so static task-success scores can be distorted by context mismatch, leakage or overfitting, evaluator defects, environmental state, uncontrolled cost and absent uncertainty estimates. They consequently call for validated scoring, reproducible and controlled protocols, realistic or held-out tasks, cost-aware comparisons, trajectory-level diagnosis and separate scrutiny of automated judges. Material internal variation concerns method and emphasis rather than direction: The Law of Evaluation offers a broad methodological critique and stresses residual limits even in expanded benchmarks; TheAgentCompany supplies specific human quality controls but no performance findings in the excerpt; AI Agents That Matter adds experiments and reproduction evidence concerning cost, scoring errors, hold-outs and environmental effects; the survey synthesises a wider literature and extends evaluation to safety, attribution and operational viability; and Agent-as-a-Judge proposes scalable intermediate evaluation but does not quantitatively validate the judge in the supplied material. Thus, automated judging is presented as a promising evaluation mechanism, not as established assurance. This characterisation applies only to the curated sources supplied, not academia or research generally.

qs.q: Without reproducible agent evaluation, it is hard to distinguish genuine improvements in agent designs from artifacts of the differences in evaluation choices.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Future work should develop controlled evaluation protocols that vary each factor independently, enabling systematic comparison and isolating the contribution of individual components, whether LLM capabilities, harness design, or specific modules such as memory or planning, to overall agent performance.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The selected regulatory, professional and policy-oriented sources accept the proposition that protocol scores are not, by themselves, evidence of competence, safety or deployment readiness, and they materially develop the evaluation framework around it. Their common reasoning is that benchmark meaning depends on choices beyond the headline score: protocol design, validation, uncertainty, evaluator quality, transparency and real-world relevance. NIST contributes operational guidance by treating test coverage and repeated trials as budget–statistical-power trade-offs and by identifying an LLM judge’s design and quality as a separate source of evaluation validity. The interdisciplinary review adds a governance layer: benchmarks should be documented, dynamically maintained and complemented by methods such as red-teaming and bug-bounty programmes because benchmark-only assurance is inadequate. There is material variation in emphasis rather than direction. NIST is narrowly methodological and does not itself make broad claims about professional competence or policy sufficiency; the interdisciplinary review focuses more directly on safety assurance, stakeholder incentives and policymakers’ ability to shape model development, while giving less attention to operating cost, statistical uncertainty and separate judge evaluation. These curated sources should not be taken as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: Having models attempt each item multiple times increases evaluation cost but can reduce uncertainty of evaluation results and enable an evaluator to quantify what portion of the uncertainty stems from model sampling.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the principal proposition that agent benchmark scores are protocol-dependent and do not by themselves establish practical competence or deployment readiness. They materially develop that proposition in complementary ways. AI Agents That Matter provides the strongest empirical and methodological extension: reproduction studies and case analyses show that evaluation choices, scoring errors, environmental state, absent hold-outs and uncontrolled inference spending can distort comparisons; it therefore calls for reproducibility, cost controls, unseen-task testing and evaluation matched to the intended level of human supervision. TheAgentCompany contributes concrete benchmark quality controls—including evaluator-validity evidence, code review, manual checking and independent review of checkpoint weights—but the supplied excerpt reports procedures rather than results proving that those controls yield valid competence measures. Agent-as-a-Judge extends evaluation toward scalable, intermediate diagnosis and more realistic coding tasks, while only claiming cost-effectiveness and richer feedback; the supplied material does not quantitatively validate the automated judge. The main internal variation is thus evidential and methodological rather than directional: one source diagnoses benchmark failures through experiments and reproductions, one specifies human quality-assurance procedures, and one proposes automated judging whose reliability remains to be established. None of these selected sources treats leaderboard performance as sufficient assurance, although they differ over whether the immediate priority is benchmark standardisation, stronger human validation or scalable automated evaluation.

qs.q: Without reproducible agent evaluation, it is hard to distinguish genuine improvements in agent designs from artifacts of the differences in evaluation choices.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: After creating all tasks, a final round of manual human double-check of required environment data, evaluator behavior, and checkpoint scoring for every task is performed to ensure quality.
qs.a: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks · Academia · 2024

elens.an: Within this curated 2025 pairing, the sources accept the proposition that protocol scores alone do not demonstrate agent competence, safety or readiness for adoption at scale. Their common reasoning is that static or aggregate task-success measures omit consequential features of real deployment: sequential interaction in changing environments, failure trajectories, policy compliance, operating and evaluation costs, and benchmark validity over time. Collectively they build on the proposition because the agent-evaluation survey supplies concrete technical requirements for controlled attribution, dynamic testing, fine-grained diagnosis and separate scrutiny of LLM judges, while the interdisciplinary review extends the argument into governance through transparency, continuing validation, real-world coverage, red-teaming and bug-bounty programmes. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis and evidential basis: the survey synthesises technical benchmark literature and addresses cost and judge reliability directly; the interdisciplinary review is a policy-oriented meta-review that stresses benchmark-only assurance and stakeholder incentives but does not materially develop the proposition’s statistical-uncertainty or automated-judge components. Neither source presents direct evidence that these proposed evaluation reforms are sufficient for adoption at scale, and the survey explicitly characterises parts of its agenda as provisional.

qs.q: Such evaluation must go beyond measuring LLM textual outputs to assess an agent’s capacity for sequential decision-making and operation within dynamic environments.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.

elens.an: The current-wave sources collectively accept the proposition that agent-benchmark scores are protocol-dependent and cannot alone establish competence or deployment readiness. They also materially develop it in two directions. NIST specifies concrete protocol controls: evaluators should balance test coverage and repeated trials against budget, use repetition to quantify sampling uncertainty, and separately scrutinise LLM judges because judge design affects the meaning of scores. The Law of Evaluation broadens the validity critique beyond protocol mechanics, arguing that static tests omit interaction, adversarial conditions and drift, while context mismatch, leakage and saturation can weaken the connection between benchmark results and deployed performance. Material internal variation lies mainly in evidentiary contribution and emphasis: NIST offers operational methodological guidance; The Law of Evaluation advances a broader governance-oriented argument and stresses residual limits even in more holistic benchmarks; the supplied Xpertbench excerpt is only bibliographic and therefore provides no determinable substantive position. Because this is a curated set, these relationships should not be read as indicating how prevalent these views are among current sources generally.

qs.q: Having models attempt each item multiple times increases evaluation cost but can reduce uncertainty of evaluation results and enable an evaluator to quantify what portion of the uncertainty stems from model sampling.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: First, because benchmarks evaluate for static outputs, they are unable to capture real usage conditions, including user interactions, adversarial inputs, or model and data drift, all of which are increasingly important for evaluation of multimodal AI applications in the wild.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026
